text:
Peter Holtz: quick q for infra folks: we’re using GPU util as one of the capacity signals feeding routing/breakers, but it feels… noisy + late. Under spike we see p99 blow up and queue depth already huge before “util” crosses threshold. Are we trusting the right thing here? how fast do these signals propagate end-to-end?

Rafael Mendes: yeah +1. in the incident last week it looked like util was ~65-70% while requests were timing out. queue depth was screaming but breaker didn’t open until much later.

Elena Popov: util is tricky because (a) smoothed, (b) sampled, (c) depends on kernel mix. If we’re using DCGM util averaged over 1m, you can be dead before it moves. Queue depth is more directly correlated with tail latency / admission.

Ravi Menon: what are the current intervals? I thought we were scraping every 15s + doing a 1m rate.

Caleb Johnson: current pipeline (prom -> remote write -> metrics service -> routing) is:
- scrape: 15s
- remote-write batch: ~5s
- ingest + downsample: 10-20s depending on load
- routing poll: every 10s
So best case ~25-35s, worst case ~60s. (Also if routing is querying a 1m rollup, add more lag.)

Peter Holtz: oof. 30-60s is basically “after the fire” for step-function spikes.

Christine Wong: that matches what we saw during load tests. util-based breaker input opened too late and then stayed open too long due to hysteresis being tuned for slower signals.

Logan Wright: also worth noting: GPU util as a single number lies when you’re memory-bound / KV cache thrash. You can have low “compute util” but still be saturated on memory bandwidth / allocator churn. Queue depth + scheduler backlog is more truthful.

Sofia Ivanova: runtime perspective: queue depth at runtime scheduler boundary is the best early warning. We can report:
- `inflight_requests`
- `prefill_queue_depth`
- `decode_queue_depth`
- `estimated_time_to_first_token_ms` (EWMA)
Those move immediately (sub-second). GPU util is retrospective.

Noah Patel: +1. For decode-heavy workloads, util fluctuates a ton. Also micro-batching can keep util “high” while latency is fine, and vice versa.

Vikram Singh: infra side: DCGM exporter reports util at 1s cadence but we’re not consuming it at 1s. Our dashboards show 15s/1m aggregations. We *could* build a fast path signal.

Rafael Mendes: question: can routing consume a push-based “pool health” signal rather than polling metrics? Something like pool agent publishes a health bit + queue depth watermark every second.

Benji Okafor: we can, but need to be careful with blast radius/cardinality. If we push per-GPU signals to routing, that’s a lot of churn. But per-pool/per-model-class rollups are manageable.

Elena Popov: I’d suggest: routing breaker inputs should be:
1) runtime queue depth / backlog (primary)
2) request error rate from runtime (timeouts/cancels) (secondary)
3) GPU util (tertiary / for “slow burn” capacity issues)
And we should use the fastest available channel for (1).

Ravi Menon: agreed. We need a clear contract: signal freshness + semantics. If we keep using metrics pipeline, we should treat it as “slow signal” only.

Caleb Johnson: we can tag each signal with `observed_at` and compute staleness at routing. Right now routing just sees the latest datapoint and assumes it’s “now”.

Christine Wong: staleness-aware breaker input would help avoid flapping too (don’t close breaker because util dropped, when the datapoint is 45s old).

Peter Holtz: what about queue depth from control plane vs runtime? control plane queue is before routing, runtime queue is after scheduling. Which one’s better?

Sofia Ivanova: runtime queue depth is the ground truth for “are GPUs actually backed up”. Control plane queue depth is useful for edge shedding but can be inflated by client retries / routing delays.

Logan Wright: also control plane queue depth can spike if routing is slow (self-inflicted), which might cause us to shed more and spiral. Using runtime queue isolates that.

Rafael Mendes: so action item: get a “fast path” runtime-to-routing capacity feed for per-(model, region, tier) pool backlog.

Vikram Singh: we can piggyback on the existing pool heartbeat channel (the one used for draining). It’s gRPC streaming already. Add fields for `decode_backlog` and `prefill_backlog` + maybe a `shed_hint` boolean.

Benji Okafor: if we do that, we should gate/feature-flag in routing so we can compare vs metrics-based signals. Also need default behavior when feed goes stale (treat as unhealthy? or ignore and fall back to metrics?).

Ravi Menon: default should probably be conservative: if fast feed is stale >N seconds, treat as unknown and fall back to metrics; don’t auto-open breaker solely due to missing signal (unless we’re already in degraded mode).

Christine Wong: +1. Otherwise a feed outage becomes a self-inflicted outage.

Caleb Johnson: we can add an explicit `capacity_signal_source` label in routing logs/traces (`fast_feed` vs `metrics`) so we can correlate with shed decisions.

Peter Holtz: do we have numbers on how predictive queue depth is vs util? (like lead time)

Sofia Ivanova: from staging load tests last week: queue depth crossed “bad” threshold ~3-5s after spike. util crossed 80% ~40-70s after spike depending on window. TTFT EWMA started climbing within ~2s.

Elena Popov: that’s exactly what we need for breakers: fast open, slower close. Use queue depth to open quickly, and maybe use a slower signal (util / backlog decay) to close with hysteresis.

Rafael Mendes: yes: open on fast signal, close on slow signal (or sustained fast signal recovery). Otherwise you get oscillation.

Logan Wright: note: queue depth thresholds have to be model-specific-ish (decode token rate varies). But we can normalize as “queueing delay estimate” rather than raw queue depth.

Noah Patel: we can compute `queueing_delay_ms = backlog_tokens / estimated_tokens_per_s` per pool. That’s a better invariant.

Peter Holtz: ok this is helpful. can someone drop links to current dashboard panels / metrics names so we align?

Caleb Johnson: Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/overload-capacity/pool-signals (panel “GPU util (1m)” vs “runtime decode backlog”). Current metrics:
- `runtime_scheduler_decode_queue_depth{region,model_pool}`
- `runtime_scheduler_prefill_queue_depth{region,model_pool}`
- `dcgm_gpu_utilization{region,gpu_pool}`
Routing currently consumes: `gpu_pool_utilization_1m` (derived) and `gpu_pool_queue_depth` (control plane).

Christine Wong: :thumbsup: I’ll open a follow-up to update breaker inputs / document “signal freshness” expectations. Also going to add a note to the thresholds working doc that util is not a fast trigger.

Vikram Singh: I’ll sync with Noah/Sofia on what we can safely add to heartbeat payload + expected update rate. If we can get 1s updates, propagation should be <2s to routing (no prometheus).

Benji Okafor: please make sure payload is bounded (no per-GPU fields). Per pool only.

Rafael Mendes: and we should add an alert for “capacity feed stale” so oncall knows we’re flying blind.

Logan Wright: +1. also add to runbook: if fast feed is down, expect breakers to respond slower and consider enabling more aggressive edge shedding.

Peter Holtz: cool. thanks all. I’ll capture summary:
- GPU util is laggy + misleading (esp memory-bound)
- metrics pipeline adds 30-60s latency today
- prioritize runtime backlog/queueing delay as primary breaker input
- add fast path via heartbeat stream; make routing staleness-aware + fallback to metrics

Christine Wong: yup. :white_check_mark:
